extracted.intended_audience: Contributors to the Metamath Proof Explorer / set.mm (authors of theorems, proofs, definitions, and maintainers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conventions for writing, labeling, formatting, and submitting axioms, definitions, theorems, and proofs to the Metamath Proof Explorer (set.mm). Covers notation, proof size, definition rules, labels/suffixes, HTML/LaTeX output, and repository contribution process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, the notation attempts to conform to modern conventions, with variations due to our choice of the axiom system or to make proofs shorter. Notation is strictly sequential (left-to-right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: summation written Σ k ∈ A B (df-sum) meaning index k ranges over A when evaluating B; Σ k∈ℕ (1/(2↑k)) = 1. Notation is usually explained in more detail when first introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic assertions ($a).
rubrics_metrics.description: All axiomatic assertions ($a statements) starting with '⊢' have labels starting with 'ax-' (axioms) or 'df-' (definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement with 'ax-' corresponds to a traditional axiom; 'df-' introduces new symbols or relationships that can be eliminated. Metamath treats $a statements as given facts; mmj2 will justify definitions except for a few that need manual metalogical justification (df-bi, df-clab, df-cleq, df-clel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proven axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a proven assertion is reintroduced as an axiom for convenience so later theorems can reference it directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convention: use regular 'ax-NAME' label for the axiom but precede it with a proof labeled 'axNAME' (example: ax-1cn proven by ax1cn). Metamath program warns if axiom does not match preceding theorem when names match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions (df-...)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage definitions to include hypertext links to proven examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should extend the definition of a wff or class and be eliminable; link to examples to help readers understand usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements with hypotheses (display conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When displayed in summarized form, hypotheses are connected with an ampersand and separated from the conclusion with a double right arrow (e.g., '⊢ φ & ⊢ (φ → ψ) ⇒ ⊢ ψ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These symbols are informal notation meaning 'and' and 'implies' and are not part of the Metamath language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discouraged use and modification
rubrics_metrics.description: If something should only be used in limited ways, it is marked with '(New usage is discouraged.)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when a construct can be made in more than one way and you don't want later theorems to depend on a specific construction, or when a proof should not normally be changed. Examples: prefer ax-1cn (proven axiom) over ax1cn (original theorem); alternate or pedagogical proofs may be marked '(Proof modification is discouraged.)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: New definitions infrequent
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new definitions only when they clearly reduce symbols, shorten proofs, or otherwise provide clear advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous definitions because each requires associated theorems and additional elimination steps. Prefer readable constructions that don't multiply definitions unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing axiom dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer proofs that depend on fewer and/or weaker axioms, even if longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid use of strong non-constructive axioms like the axiom of choice (df-ac) where possible; prefer weaker variants (countable choice ax-cc or dependent choice ax-dc). Example: Schroeder-Bernstein proof avoiding axiom of choice. Do not similarly reduce dependencies on definitions since definitions are conservative, except for certain definition-acts noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate proofs (ALT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a different proof is shorter or clearer but uses stronger axioms, mark it as an alternate proof with an 'ALT' suffix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate proof comment should begin with 'Alternate proof of ~ xxx' and describe specificity. Alternate proofs should have '(Proof modification is discouraged.) (New usage is discouraged.)' in their comment and follow the main statement; comments should link to each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate versions (ALTV)
rubrics_metrics.description: ALTV suffix reserved for theorems/definitions which are alternate versions or variants of an existing theorem (typically in mathboxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used temporarily until the preferred variant is chosen; if both variants are kept, rename with a more explicit suffix indicating how it varies; comments should link to the main version and describe differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old (OLD) versions or proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When removing a proof/definition/axiom, stage the change by renaming its label with an OLD suffix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OLD statements should have '(Proof modification is discouraged.) (New usage is discouraged.)' and 'Obsolete version of ~ xxx as of dd-Mmm-yyyy.' in the comment. Old statement should follow the main statement; typically keep old proof for one year when a shorter proof is found (except when the minimize command shortened it automatically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variables (naming and ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for representing variables: propositional (wff) variables use lowercase Greek in a preferred order; individual setvar variables use lowercase Latin in order; class variables often uppercase Latin in alphabetical order starting from A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: φ, ψ, χ, θ, τ, η, ζ, σ for wffs; x, y, z, w, v, u, t for setvars; A, B, C... for classes. Surreal number section uses subscripted lowercase Latin x_O, x_L, x_R. Some special symbols used as class variables (0 for zero element, + for group addition) and selection may vary to improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnstile
rubrics_metrics.description: '⊢', meaning 'It is provable that', is the first token of all assertions and hypotheses that aren't syntax constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents ambiguity with syntax constructions (e.g., 'wff ¬ φ'). Using ⊢ as the first token follows standard logic convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (↔) handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches to maximizing effectiveness of biconditionals: (1) produce biconditionals via one-directional simplifications, or (2) have one-directional simplifications that consume biconditionals. set.mm follows the second approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically: for theorems that use an implication in the hypothesis, provide corresponding versions with a biconditional or reversed biconditional (mpbi, mpbir). This keeps duplication bounded by propositional calculus size rather than number of later theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers (naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiers are named: ∀ : wal (1540); ∃ : df-ex (1782); ∃* : df-mo (2540); ∃! : df-eu (2570).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrase 'uniqueness quantifier' since ambiguous; prefer explicit symbol notation and the listed labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression '[y/x]φ' should be read 'the formula that results from the proper substitution of y for x in the formula φ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See df-sb and related df-sbc and df-csb for formal treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is-a-set
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A ∈ V' should be read 'Class A is a set (i.e., exists)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using A ∈ 𝑉 (variable) to make statements more general and avoid extra substitutions; for $e hypotheses of theorems in inference form, however, use '⊢ A ∈ V' rather than '⊢ A ∈ 𝑉'. For deduction-form antecedents, use '⊢ (φ → A ∈ 𝑉)' rather than '⊢ (φ → A ∈ V)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse symbol (◡)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbol '◡' denotes the converse of a relation: '◡ R' denotes the converse of class R (usually a relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid denoting converse by R^-1 because it is not generally a genuine inverse; examples show where inverse properties hold in specific contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function application notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbols 'F' x' should be read as 'the value of (function) F at x' and have same meaning as F(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Left apostrophe (prime) notation originated with Peano; ASCII representation has spaces around grave accent. See df-fv and examples like (cos'0) = 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infix and parentheses conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function taking two classes is applied as part of an infix expression, the expression is always surrounded by parentheses. Predicate expressions in infix form producing wffs are also always surrounded by parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (2 + 2); (φ → ψ), (φ ∨ ψ), (φ ∧ ψ), (φ ↔ ψ). In contrast, binary relations comparing two classes producing a wff are not surrounded by parentheses (e.g., A ∈ B, A = B, A ⊆ B, A < B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unary minus
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '-' to indicate unary minus (e.g., -1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unary minus is specially defined because it is commonly used; see cneg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function definition pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Define functions by first defining the constant symbol ($c) and declaring it a class with cNAME, then define the function with df-NAME using maps-to notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also provide closure proofs (NAMEcl), function application forms (NAMEval), and at least one simple value example. Recursive definitions are another route (df-ack example for Ackermann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat factorial as a normal function applied in prefix form rather than traditional postfix notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (!'4) = 24 (df-fac, fac4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguous symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A given symbol must have a single unambiguous meaning in general; when literature reuses a symbol for different meanings we use distinct variant symbols (suffixes, subscripts, underlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '0' always means df-0, '0g' is group identity, '0.' poset zero, '0_p' zero polynomial, '0vec' zero vector. Use different tokens to remove ambiguity even if visually similar to standard notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASCII representation of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Each symbol must have an ASCII representation; choose short sequences (ideally digraphs) resembling the mathematical symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include parentheses inside a symbol. Greek letters for wff variables use first two letters of English names. Symbols like ∀ are represented by 'A.'; ∈ by 'e.'; ∃ by 'E.'; single-letter constants are usually prefixed with '_' in ASCII (e.g., '_i' for imaginary unit i). Script font constants often use '~P' for 𝒫. Variables may use variants like '.+' to represent '+'-like tokens for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing tokens for advanced concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting ASCII tokens for advanced concepts (no standard symbols) is challenging; favor readable short abbreviations while balancing length and crypticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Grp' for group, 'Top' for topology; there is no universal standard and community consensus would be helpful. Convention: start tokens with capital letter for collection-like objects and lower case for function-like objects when possible (e.g., On, Fin, Grp vs sin, tan, log).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Class symbols for functions (e.g., abs, sin) should usually not have leading/trailing blanks in HTML; class symbols for operations (e.g., gcd, sadd, eval) usually include blanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a class symbol is used both as function and operation, use the convention appropriate for its primary usage (examples: (iEdg' G) vs (V iEdg E) for edges of a graph).

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each token has a 'LaTeX definition' used by the Metamath program to output TeX files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors should favor simplicity over perfect display and only use core LaTeX symbols or symbols from standard packages (amssymb, amsmath, mathtools, mathrsfs, phonetic). If other packages are needed, discuss first. Useful resource: The Comprehensive LaTeX Symbol List.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number construction independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid proofs that depend on specific set-theoretic constructions of number systems; reintroduce complex number postulates as axioms after deriving them from set theory to be independent of construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow construction-specific facts such as '∅ ∉ ℂ' that would break portability; keep proofs about ℂ independent of particular construction choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases minimize hypotheses so statements are more general and easier to use, but add hypotheses when they increase portability or explicitly state domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for adding hypotheses: clarify intended domain (ℝ, ℝ*, ω, etc.), force intended use, avoid brittle out-of-domain coincidences. Consensus in the group favors sometimes keeping redundant hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural numbers conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ℕ (df-nn) for positive integers starting from 1 and ℕ0 (df-n0) for nonnegative integers starting at zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention differences in literature and be explicit which convention is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal number constructor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use decimal constructor df-dec for base-10 numeric literals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: represent numbers larger than nine using decimal constructor; e.g., 4001 is representable and provably prime (4001prm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem forms (closed, deduction, inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify theorems as 'closed form' (no $e hypotheses), 'deduction form' (hypotheses and conclusion are implications that share same antecedent), or 'inference form' (one or more $e hypotheses but not deduction form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer deduction form (deduction style) to emulate Deduction Theorem use; use label suffixes: 'd' for deductions, 'i' for inferences, none or 't' for closed theorems. When converting inferences with 'is a set' hypotheses to closed form, sometimes suffix 'g' is used for 'more general'. When submitting new theorems, prefer general form without 'g' suffix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction theorem (practical emulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction Theorem is a metatheorem providing an algorithm to construct a theorem from its deduction, but it is not applied directly in Metamath because of step explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives: use 'weak deduction theorem' (dedth) or dedhb in certain cases; primary mechanism is to write proofs in deduction form (deduction style) so φ → mimics context. See mmnatded for translations and natded list for common natural deduction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursion (defining recursive functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define recursive functions using recursion constructors (recs(F), rec(F,I), seqω(F,I), seqM(+,F)) that allow compact direct definitions and simpler proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructors reduce risk of unsound definitions and produce compact definitions; df-recs is primary logically, df-seq is most useful for average user when countable sequences suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensible structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'extensible structure' used to represent structures (ring, group, poset, etc.) so theorems about general structures can be reused for specialized structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use df-struct to enable reuse without reproof for specialized structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undefined results and 'junk theorems'
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle expressions that are only meaningful in certain contexts either by making them evaluate to the empty set outside expected context or marking constructs as discouraged and proving only specific permitted properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach 1: evaluate to empty set when outside expected context (Quine style iota). Useful for reverse-closure theorems and to shorten proofs. Approach 2: use '(New usage is discouraged.)' on constructs and only prove intended properties. Avoid definitions that break equality or other metatheorems. Avoid syntactic invalidation approaches that complicate parsing or make parsing undecidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing proofs (lemmas and reuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break longer proofs into smaller parts; create separate proofs of reusable results to help readers and reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemmas supporting a final proof should use naming convention final_label + 'lem' (e.g., sbthlem1 is lemma for sbth). Lemma comment should begin with 'Lemma for' and the final proof label so they can be suppressed in theorem lists. Consider proving reusable results separately so others can reuse them easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit proof size
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer breaking longer proofs into smaller parts; encourage proofs to be no more than 200 essential steps and generally no more than 500 essential steps (guideline, not strict).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: human readability, minimize mm-pa minimize command runtime, and encourage reuse. Autogenerated proofs may be exceptions when breaking up is inefficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof stubs and incomplete work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept proofs with unknown steps in the public database. For partial results, you may temporarily define a claim as an axiom with an explicit comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If temporarily providing a claim as an axiom, include 'Temporarily provided as axiom' in its comment; incomplete work generally accepted only in a mathbox. Using '?' in proofs is allowed in personal copies but proofs with '?' fail verification and are not accepted publicly. Avoid 'sorry' style axioms in the public database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertext links in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should include many links to related material with explanatory text to help readers understand context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tilde-prefixed references (e.g., ' ~ df-prm ' ) in ASCII source to insert links; the Metamath program auto-inserts links for syntax, axioms, definitions, proof justifications, and next/previous assertions. Links to HTTP/HTTPS or mm-scheme can be inserted similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertext links to section headers (note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some section headers have explanatory text but are not part of axioms/theorem descriptions and there is no direct link to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide links elsewhere or use relative links (e.g., mmcomplex.html) to reference related pages; be aware of linking limitations to header-only sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography references (strict format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include bibliographic reference to any external material used. Names in square brackets indicate bibliography references and must follow a strict format requiring page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full reference format: KEYWORD IDENTIFIER? NOISEWORD(S)* [AUTHOR(S)] p. NUMBER - where KEYWORD must be one of a specified list (Axiom, Chapter, Compare, Condition, Corollary, Definition, Equation, Example, Exercise, Figure, Item, Lemma, Lemmas, Line, Lines, Notation, Part, Postulate, Problem, Property, Proposition, Remark, Rule, Scheme, Section, or Theorem). IDENTIFIER optional, NOISEWORDS from 'from,in,of,on'. AUTHOR must be present in mmset.html bibliography anchors. Page numbers are required for individual $a or $p statements; references without page numbers allowed only in heading comments. New references should be added to Bibliography section of mmset.html; mmbiblio.html is auto-rebuilt by MM> WRITE BIBLIOGRAPHY.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable shorter proofs (criteria for acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorter proofs that satisfy certain criteria will usually be automatically accepted and acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually automatically accept shorter proofs that (1) shorten set.mm file (with compressed proofs), (2) reduce generated HTML file size, (3) use only existing, unmodified theorems in the database, and (4) use no additional axioms. Preference is given to reduced compressed proof steps over label section length; tie-breakers include fewer different labels or fewer symbols in proof display. Community may override for aesthetic or non-technical reasons. For some theorems with intentionally longer proofs to avoid certain axioms or for pedagogy, include $j usage comments indicating avoided axioms; shorter proofs violating these criteria won't be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information on syntax, axioms, and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hyperlinked list of syntax, axioms, and definitions, refer to mmdefinitions.html.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have questions about a specific symbol or axiom, go directly to its definition; generated HTML for each theorem/axiom includes links to each symbol's definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved symbols: 'LETTER
rubrics_metrics.description: Some symbols are reserved for potential future use: symbols with pattern 'LETTER are reserved for possibly representing characters (similar to Lisp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect usages like '\n' for newline, 'sp for space, maybe '\x24 for dollar; avoid using these reserved patterns for other purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The challenge of varying mathematical conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When literature uses differing conventions, pick a reasonably common convention and stick to it; acknowledge impossibility of pleasing everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: conventions for metavariables representing arbitrary wffs vary (open phi φ, closed phi ϕ, Greek αβγ, Roman A B C, script, italic, fraktur). Document and list conventions and source texts that use them to justify choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness or freeness conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions addressing distinctness or freeness: Ⅎ x φ read 'x is not free in φ'; $d x y read 'Assume x and y are distinct variables', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $d φ x read 'Assume x does not occur in φ'. Sometimes Ⅎ x φ is used instead of $d φ x for more general results; ordering conventions: class and wff variables should appear at beginning of distinct variable conditions, setvars in alphabetical order. Provide technique to replace $d conditions with Ⅎ forms via dummy variable substitution and use of chvar/mpbir as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional rules for definitions (conservativity and eliminability checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard Metamath verifiers do not distinguish axioms and definitions, but set.mm requires definitions to be conservative and eliminable; additional rules are applied to almost all definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition-check rules (summary): (1) expression must be biconditional or equality (root-symbol ↔ or =); (2) definiendum is LHS, definiens RHS; (3) defined expression must not appear in any statement between its syntax axiom and its definition and must not be used in its definiens; (4) no two variables in LHS may share a DV (disjoint variable) condition; (5) all dummy variables (vars occurring in RHS but not LHS) must be disjoint from any other variable in the labeled expression; (6) either (a) no non-setvar dummy variables, or (b) justification theorem required of form '⊢ (definiens root-symbol definiens')' where dummy variables are replaced with unused dummy variables of same type; (7) for setvar dummy variables, either no setvar dummy variables, or a justification theorem as in rule 6, or every setvar dummy must not be free (i.e., φ → ∀x φ provable), with two different nonfreeness tests available (syntactic binding fast-test or proof search for (φ → ∀x φ)). Also note: justification theorem must be proven before the dependent definition; examples given (vjust for df-v). These checks are implemented in mmj2's definitionCheck and rely on database structure similar to set.mm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple verifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire file is verified by multiple independently-implemented verifiers when checked in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides extremely high confidence that all proofs follow from assumptions; checkers also detect problems like overly long lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discouraged information (tracking)
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate file named 'discouraged' lists all discouraged statements and uses, and is checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you change use of discouraged things you must update that file; this highlights changes and triggers further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: LRParser check (unambiguous parsing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that the database unambiguously parse using an LRParser check to avoid syntactic ambiguity that Metamath language alone permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LRParser check implemented in mmj2 (source path given). This counters malicious or devious ambiguous constructs (example referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposing specific changes (contribution process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose specific changes as pull requests against the 'develop' branch of set.mm on GitHub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repository: https://github.com/metamath/set.mm/tree/develop. Use PRs rather than unspecified patches; include clear descriptions and links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community (participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage anyone interested in Metamath to join the mailing list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mailing list: https://groups.google.com/g/metamath. Page includes contributor/revision metadata (dates, revision comments, discouraged tags).
